en: ÊVādhūla ZS 11 Aśvamedha [ṛecheck M from M378(11.18)] Ê [Note: This provisional text is intended to provide the exact readings of all available manuscripts that are worth consulting as a basis for preparing a new critical edition; thus, it represents only a preliminary stage requiring extensive revision from both stylistic and lexical perspectives.]
Regarding the *saṃdhis* that differ from the standard northern convention commonly adopted in ordinary editions, see the introduction to VadhZS 1.1–1.4, *Zinbun* 30.

[In all manuscripts, this *prapāṭhaka* begins abruptly following a lacuna, and there is no explicit mark indicating its commencement; however, the text itself clearly indicates the beginning of the *Aśvamedha* *prapāṭhaka*.]
When a victorious king, intending to perform the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*), has no affliction from any quarter whatsoever, he should, one year prior, [perform the rite] for the month of Phālguna.

On the full moon day, he dispatches four mule-chariots, saying: "Rally the sixteen provinces! Each chariot is accompanied by four [attendants]. He who dispatches one toward the east goes to the rival king who is situated in the front and says to him: "So-and-so, the son of such-and-such, will perform the horse sacrifice; give him your permission."
If he permits that, he sends him to another; he sends that one to another, and that one to yet another; likewise toward the south, likewise toward the west, and likewise toward the north.

Then, after four months, he sends it forth during the rainy season at the time of the *āśvattha* [full moon]; they say this very thing: "That which has been sent forth twice indeed consists of four months. Then, after another four months, he sends it forth on the full moon day of *kārttika*; they say this very thing: "That which has been sent forth thrice indeed consists of eight months."

Then, after two months from that, he sends [the messengers] on the full moon of Taiṣya; they say this very thing; that indeed— [Note: K1 wishes to delete the following underlined passage and place it in parentheses; K4 retains it, but M and C do not adopt it].

Three [messages] have been sent during eight months; then, after that, he sends two during two months, so that four [messages] have been sent during ten months. Of those, whoever approves it day after day, he understands it accordingly.

Now, regarding him whom he does not permit—whom he intends to overcome, whom he thinks he will conquer by force—he exerts himself against him. But regarding him whom he does not intend to overcome, whom he does not think he will conquer by force, they bring him tribute; or else, they seek to win him over with wealth, whether it be his sister or his daughter.

Then, during the next two months, he carries this [sacrificial ground] for the people until his conquest by arrows is complete, as far as the extent of the *śāsīṣāvit*—that is, the sacrificial ground (*devayajana*) which encompasses it on all sides, measuring one *yojana* both [long and wide] from the sacrificial ground; they level the ground between those [limits], and whatever stump remains there, they cut it down.

Regarding this, they say: "There should be two ponds that are flowing, named auspiciously, and not drying up. Now, they also ask: "How might one find those two which are flowing, named auspiciously, and not drying up? One should have these very two dug out; that indeed performs the ritual act, just as...

Moreover, they split those two apart and assign auspicious names to them; those two become flowing, possessing auspicious names, and non-failing. Behind the sacrificial ground (*devayajana*) is where they erect these two *śālā* (halls): the southern one at the sacrificial ground and the other to the north.
At those two southern doors, they construct eight water-channels in the shed, which has its rafters facing north; the other southern [channel] is from the south.

This is the full moon day of Phālguna; having sacrificed on it, he remains for the subsequent half-month performing only sacrificial rites, gathering what is required: namely, whichever among his horses is the best and by whom he is celebrated—if that horse, being celebrated, should be of two colors:

They say that these two forms—white and black—constitute day and night, for they say, "This is the form of day and night. And they say, "This is indeed he who shines yonder," for it is he who is perceived directly; indeed, it is he who is obtained.

A turban made of woolen threads (*kuśorṇa*) is twelve *aratnis* long when stretched forward and thirteen across; it is wound around the horse's halter (*aśvābhidhānī*) made of muñja grass. This very [turban] serves as the vessel for the horse's halter for the sake of stability; the other [halter] belongs to the old horse, the one who has ceased his work, and to the son of a younger wife who is to receive her dowry.

And [the following]: *kṛṣṇaḥ śvā*, *kṛṣṇaś ca caturakṣaḥ*, *viṣvagbaddhaś ca gardūlaḥ*, *pauṃścaleyaś ca*, *kadvac ca musalaḥ*, *jaratpūrvā ca*, *eṣīkaś codūhaḥ*. This *udūha* is as large as the great *avasrāva* is.
In that [structure], it is bound with reed branches and covered with long ropes at both ends; and there are four hundred men [to hold it].

A hundred royal princes, a hundred kings, a hundred charioteers and village chiefs, a hundred chamberlains and collectors, and two—the Brāhmaṇa and the Rājanya—who sing the *gāthās* on the *vīṇā* while the two of them, with crooked and tawny heads, perform; and the fourfold waters: those of the Sarasvatī, the flowing ones, the swelling ones, and the roaring ones; and the hide of a bull and the hide of a tiger.

And there are two gold pieces—one of silver and one of gold—and two others: gold and silver. Or there are four *sāhasra* weights, or one weighing a hundred *pala*. For the initiation for the *adhvara*, the *kṛṣṇala* weights, and those materials required for the initiation for the *agni*, both sets of these are prepared for him; he reaches that new-moon day among them.

Having performed the Sāṃgrahaṇī sacrifice with the thought, "May I win over these people," he sacrifices. Having sacrificed and performed the ritual conclusion (*udavasāna*) according to the procedure for the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*), [he performs the rites].

Or, having driven forward a *prājāpatya* bull, he sacrifices a hornless, multi-colored *prājāpatya* bull for the sake of all desires. Having washed its hide and cut it up, they set it aside; this is the second [hide] for the tiger-skin. Now, before the sixth [day], the two *prājāpatya* [oblations] are offered; [the Adhvaryu] offers six [portions] to the *Bharata*... the *Āgnīdhra* [performs] the *samāna*...

[11] They two enter upon the Prājāpatya [rite]. He collects the materials for six days; when the nights have passed, they enter upon the fire-laying ceremony. The King (Soma) is on the south, the [Pu... on the north.

Having drawn lines in three directions and sprinkled [water], the domestic priest churns the *gārhapatya* fire and carries forth the *āhavanīya*; they carry forth the *anvāhāryapacana*. Having spread the fires, the domestic priest goes around the front of the fires and sits down to the south of the king, near the fires. Having strewn [grass] around them... having filled the *sruva* ladle... having sat down... having strewn [grass] around them... having filled the *sruva* ladle.
Having spread [the grass] and wiped the *sruva* ladle, he performs the expiation of evil from the front; some, however, perform it from below, while others perform it from both sides.

He should indeed perform the *avayaja* sacrifice. He offers oblations with a *sruva*-ladle as they occur: "To Death, svāhā! To Death, svāhā!"—thus ninety oblations; and eleven beginning with "To Prayāsa, svāhā!"—those make one hundred and one. ... (regarding the *vahatyā* and the *anubrahmaṇyā*, they say: "In former times, indeed, [the hundred and one] were joined... [Note: The text provided contains fragments of a ritual manual (*kalpa*). The bracketed portions indicate textual variants or lacunae from the manuscript sources.]

[23] "The priests of the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) bring together those who are well-prepared"—thus they say. But regarding that, they indeed say: "How could they be able to yoke them? Even if they were able to yoke them, they would certainly not be able to drive them. Those very ones which have their wombs separated (*vicittagarbhā*) after the *vaiṣuvata* day...

Indeed, after the Vaiṣuvata day, the embryos turn back toward the west; they become mothers facing westward. This very thing is the form of the eight [days]; this indeed is the form of the eight [days]. They face westward; this indeed is the form of the eight [days]. This is the form of those moving in all directions (*viṣūcīna*); these are most comfortable.

“They carry the elders”—thus they say; “bearing the embryos,” thus they say. With other [carts] they carry them from afar, but with these they carry them from nearby; thereby they bestow honor upon them. He shaves his hair and beard, trims his nails, cleanses his teeth, bathes, and puts on a new garment (or *vāsas*).

Then, when the sun has risen above the trees, he gives the command: "O *kṣattṛ*, the *brahmaudana* has been cooked and removed; it has been basted with clarified butter, and the sun has risen over it. This is merely a formal command; for by this very [formula], the disciples of the *adhvaryu* proceed.

Then, as the sun is setting, having placed gold and silver into the two openings of the mouth, they restrain their speech. Gold indeed belongs to the king, and silver to the queen; for one who has restrained his speech, they offer the *agnihotra* that night. Regarding this, they say: "A naked man should lie down with a naked woman, without any covering..."

"Let him couple at will; let him move between her thighs at will, but let him not couple. Regarding this, they say: "In this very case, one who is performing the *kārī-vayan* rite may lie naked with a naked woman, coupling without an intervening garment. This is the form for waking; they should attend upon [the fire] while keeping themselves awake. And so, they attend upon it while keeping themselves awake.

When he is about to offer the morning Agnihotra for him, he carries the two golden plates around; then they beat them together with water—the Adhvaryu beats the gold one and the Pratiprasthātṛ the silver one—and then this *brahmaudana* (the Brahmin’s rice-mess).

Having poured fourfold portions of water into the *anvāhāryapacana* fire, they cook these very [grains], pouring out handfuls of them for sprinkling. Having cooked them, he prepares a vessel (*udañcana*). Then he takes a bull’s hide; its...

He spreads out a bull’s hide with its neck to the east and the hair side up behind the fire. Upon a tiger skin, he places a vessel; upon that vessel, he spreads out a silver *rukmá*. Having set aside a golden *rukmá*, he pours this rice-mess into it without letting it spill, having made a hollow for pouring. He places a golden *rukmá* underneath and pours clarified butter over it as the presiding substance.

Then he worships the sun: "Homage to the seer, homage to the overseer, homage to the observer, homage to the proclaimer, homage to the one who proclaims nearby, homage to the one who proclaims after; homage to the existent, homage to the existent, homage to the beholder, homage to the beholder, homage to the hearer, homage to the one who hears nearby, homage to the past, homage to the future, homage to the eye, homage to the ear, homage to the mind, homage to speech, homage to Brahman."

"Salutation to austerity, salutation to peace, salutation!"—having thus spoken, while the officiating priests remain silent, the Adhvaryu sits down facing west in front; the Brahman to the south facing north; the Hotṛ behind facing east; and the Udgātṛ to the north facing south. These lumps of food remain uneaten.

Then, having moistened this horse-halter in a vessel of water and having satiated it, he places it near the door. Having consumed three mouthfuls himself, they praise him, saying, "Your *brahmaudana* has been prepared. He releases his speech, saying, "I grant a boon."

To these he gives four thousand [cows] each, or one hundred parts each; then he chooses the officiating priests (ṛtvij): with "Thou art my Adhvaryu," he chooses the Adhvaryu; with "Thou art my Brahman," the Brahman; with "Thou art my Hotṛ," the Hotṛ; with "Thou art my Udgātṛ," the Udgātṛ. He says, "O Brāhmaṇas and kings..."

"By means of this horse, by means of this sacrificial steed, may he bring it to a successful conclusion up to the state of non-Brahmanhood," they say; "With that, we bring you to a successful conclusion"—thus they declare, "up to the state of non-Brahmanhood, up to the state of non-Brahmanhood, up to the state of non-Brahmanhood," and so they agree. Then he makes the King (Soma) the Adhvaryu.

He said: "O Brahmins and kings, this Adhvaryu priest shall be your king for this year. Whatever honor is mine, that shall be his; whatever authority is mine, that shall be his. Just as you have served me, so shall you serve him. Whatever steadfastness I maintain, that shall be your steadfastness."

Having made the *adhvaryu* the king, he performs the *Āyuṣyā* sacrifice with the *Śatakṛṣṇalā* offering, [thinking]: "By this long life, may he attain well-being for this rite. Having performed the *Āyuṣyā* sacrifice with the *Śatakṛṣṇalā*, they enter the two halls from the north: the king by the southern one, the domestic priest (*purohita*) by the northern one—the king with the sacrificial formula (*yajus*), the domestic priest silently. "Ye... [K1: t.]

"O divine Savitṛ, speak of these paths as paths for those who have perished"—having thus drawn three lines, sprinkled water, and churned the *gārhapatya* fire, he carries it up to the *āhavanīya*; they carry the *ānvāhāryapacana*. Having spread the fires, the domestic priest (*purohita*), having gone around the front of the fires, stands to the south.

While the King is seated toward the west, the Adhvaryu priests attend to and establish his fires: for the Gārhapatya fire, [he says], "Homage to Agni, who dwells on earth—grant [it to me]"; for the Anvāhāryapacana fire, "Homage to Vāyu, who dwells in the intermediate space"; and for the Āhavanīya fire, "Homage to Sūrya, who dwells in heaven."

Then, having brought this horse, they station it facing east in front of the hall within the sacrificial ground (*antarvedi*). He pays homage to it with these four hundred men: one hundred princes (*rājaputra*) to the south, one hundred charioteers and village-heads (*sūtagrāmaṇī*) to the west, and one hundred attendants and collectors (*kṣattṛsaṃgrahītṛ*) to the north.

Then he gave that black, four-eyed dog, which was holding a horse covered by a rope tied all around, to his younger sister as her *anvādheya* (dowry); the first son belonged to the younger sister, and the latter to the *anvādheya*.

The son of Pauṃścaleya, having wrapped his left knee with a cloth from the front, and having placed a club made of *sīdhraka* wood upon his right shoulder, stands behind him. They bring this wooden mortar (*udūhan*) and hold it in front of him.

Then, having brought the horse's halter, they place it to the north of the Āhavanīya fire. Intending to take hold of it, he addresses the Brahman priest: "O Brahman, I shall bind the sacrificial horse for the gods and for Prajāpati; may I prosper through it. "Bind it," says the Brahman priest. "For the gods and for Prajāpati, prosper through it—prosper through it! he says.

"May you prosper!"—thus they raise their auspicious voices on all sides. Then, with the formula, "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ," he takes up the horse's halter. With "I take you for the arms of the Aśvins," he addresses it. With "They took this halter of Order; they made it ready," and "Thou art the bond," he ties the horse. "The world..."

"Thou art upon the earth; may it be well with thee for the gods, svāhā! Svāhā to thee for Prajāpati!"—saying this, they drive toward the southern bank, having honored the driver, saying, "For all beings, thee! As for that [place], these are those hundreds of men...

Hundreds of men follow after him who is without fame; he who moves about at full moon follows the dog from behind. The *adhvaryu* gives this instruction: "When they have immersed the horse up to its vital breaths (*prāṇa*), and it has reached the unstable regions, then I shall give the command and strike it. As they immerse it, they cause the horse to be immersed up to its vital breaths in the unstable regions.

When he approaches, the *adhvaryu* impels him with the words, "O Varuṇa, he who seeks to strike down the courser, he plots against the honey. With a pestle made of *saidhraka* wood, he strikes him. While it is being struck, he causes [the sacrificer] to recite, "May the mortal pass away, may he pass away! Having placed that pestle beneath the horse's foot and having caused it to float away toward the south, he [proceeds].
He assigns [the horse]; then the Adhvaryu sprinkles the horse with a hundred princes standing in front.

In front, together with a hundred princes, the *adhvaryu* [proclaims]: "Having sacrificed with this sacrificial horse, may this king slay Vṛtra. To the south, together with a hundred fierce non-kings (*arāja*), the *brahman* [proclaims]: "Having sacrificed with this sacrificial horse, may this king be invincible. To the west, together with a hundred charioteers and village headmen, the *hotṛ* [proclaims]: "Having sacrificed with this horse..."

"Having sacrificed with the *medhya* [oblation], may this king be one for whom this people is abundant—abundant indeed in sesame, abundant in elephants and gold, abundant in servants, wealthy, prosperous, and possessing great abundance of riches. With these words, the *udgātṛ* priest, together with a hundred *kṣattṛ*s and *saṃgrahītṛ*s, [should lead] this horse from the north.

Having sacrificed with the *medhya* formulas, [the Adhvaryu] sprinkles [the sacrificer] while reciting, "May the king attain a full lifespan. Thus, he indeed attains the status of a sacrificer. Then they sprinkle him while reciting this entire section beginning with, "O Brahman, may a Brāhmaṇa be born endowed with spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasī*)," up to its conclusion. They turn him toward the south; as he is being turned, he causes him to recite, "I and you, O slayer of Vṛtra..."

Then these five hundred men split into two groups: fifty of the princes—though they were not kings—joined with the charioteers and attendants; and fifty of the charioteers and village chiefs—though they were not kings—joined with the charioteers and attendants.

Two hundred women become two groups of one hundred; [then] both the Adhvaryu and the Sacrificer approach the King. The Hotṛ [approaches] the Kṣattṛ and the Saṃgrahītṛ. Then, having brought this reed raft (*aiṣīka udūha*), he places it in the eastern part of the lake. They obtain one hundred [women] for one rope, one hundred for another.

"Having struck down [the enemy], they shall press forward," he says, just as one might say, "The wave has struck the horse along with its head. Having struck down [the enemy], they press forward; while they are pressing forward, he causes [the sacrificer] to recite: "O Indra, having overcome [the enemy], advance in your heroic deed..."
Having recited, "O Indra, come with thy steeds, O Bhr̥ādhvan" (or "O Indra, come with thy steeds, O Bhr̥ādhān"), Urmim strikes the horse right at its head.

Right there, having soaked this reed-mat (*aiṣīka udūha*) in water, they lead the horse up to it. When all four of its hooves have entered [the mat], he then offers the *dhṛti* oblations into its feet: "Here is support, svāhā!"—thus on the front right foot; "Here is separation, svāhā!"—thus on the rear right foot.

He recites the latter half-verse on the northern [altar]: "May she find delight here, svāhā! and the former half-verse on the eastern [altar]: "She finds delight here, svāhā! He then recites below the *tokyā* [ladle]. Regarding this, they say: "One should recite from the last *stokā*. On this point, however, they say: "In that way, it would not be completed immediately; one should recite a thousand [verses]. Thus, he indeed recites a thousand. He [recites] this...

He recites one hundred times the *anuvāka* of the *stokīya* verses beginning with "To Agni, svāhā! To Soma, svāhā!"—these constitute the thousand *stokīyas*. Then, having led this horse in front of the *āgnīdhra* fire, they station it facing east within the sacrificial altar (*antarvedi*) in front of the hall. Four hundred men worship it. <11.7> (11.6.1) [K1,K4,74b13–; M360–; Cf. Cal. Dritte Mitt. No.74, p.179–180=KS362–3.]

[... thus] thirty [...]. Having offered the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti), whether from here or from there, while drinking the full oblation, or thereafter, one should go to the north of the hall for the ritual bath (āplavana).

Having led him there, they enclose him. Having led him there, having bathed him, having anointed him, having applied collyrium, and having purified him, they spread out the sacrificial plants and strew around the fires. Having melted the clarified butter over the *gārhapatya* fire, having purified it, and having wiped both the *sruva* and the *sruk* ladles, he goes forward to the east. Here he offers the fourfold-drawn portion (*caturgṛhīta*) into the *tānūnaptra* oblation; here he offers the fourfold-drawn portion into the *ājapeya* oblation.

(27) Here he offers the fourfold-drawn [oblation]... in the Vājapeya... here he offers in those [pressings]. [K1 adds: "He offers here in those"]. [K1: ...he offers at each pressing]; in the Vājapeya he offers at each pressing; day by day here he then performs the Agnidīkṣā offerings. He performs all the rites pertaining to the fire-altar (*agnikarma*). He does not deviate from the fire-rites. For him, the Dīkṣā offerings remain unoffered.

Then, having brought this horse forward along the front of the hall, they lead it eastward within the sacrificial ground (*antarvedi*). These four men [the *puruṣas*] mount it. He says: "The Brāhmaṇas and the kings... [He says: "The Brāhmaṇas and the kings, regarding that which they say at every step of the horse..."

[The sacrificer says: "We shall do this so that what is pure may be offered; thus we shall act so that for him there will be an offering at every step, and our ritual work will be abundant. With such resolve, he offers into his feet. By the very fact that he moves about with those feet over which the offerings have been made, by that alone [his sacrifice is accomplished].

It becomes a vessel; then he sprinkles it with fourfold water. With those waters which are placed there, he sprinkles it from the front with the formula, “For Agni thee,” and for Vāyu... [the rest of the text follows].

"To Narta and Vāyu, you!"—thus on the south; "To Indra and Agni, you!"—thus from behind; "To Prajāpati, you!"—thus on the north; "To the Gods, you!"—thus above; "To all beings, you!"—thus below. Then he offers in the collection of oblations, saying: "To Agni, svāhā! To Soma, svāhā! These [oblations] are followed by a thousand *stokyā* offerings.

With the verses beginning, “To the coming, svāhā! To the departing, svāhā!”—these are the twelve *pradrāvānī* formulas—and with “To the one for whom the sound ‘kā’ is made, svāhā! To the one for whom the syllable ‘oṃ’ is made, svāhā!”—these are the eighty-three horse-movements (*aśvacaritāni*). Then, having recited the four *dhṛti* verses, he rises up and whispers into his right ear: “Vibhūr mātā... (The Mother is all-pervading).

"Vast through thy mother, abundant through thy father, thou art manly-minded"—with these words he takes hold of the girth-rope as it is led out, saying, "Thou art named Yayu," and then releases it with, "Follow the flight of the Ādityas. Then he hands it over, saying, "Thou art Bhūḥ; for the sake of the world (bhuvaḥ), I hand thee over; thou hast been sprinkled; protect me, O protector."
For him, Jarad-aśva directs four hundred men as guards to follow after the place of rest.
He instructs them: "Do not turn back for six months while following him; whichever direction he may go, and whatever distress he may suffer, report that to me."

"Whatever cooked food I have for you, that I make savory for you; and whatever is bound crosswise by me, that has been spread out by me as it was brought forth, not that which is bound lengthwise"—it is in imitation of this that even now the horse-keepers of the Kurus take up what is bound crosswise.

"Those who say, 'This is not lawful,' it is indeed lawful for those who protected this horse. He said: "O Brahmins and kings, let your mounts depart! Whosever mount this horse shall approach, he shall suffer total loss."

Against their neighboring kingdoms, an invasion breaks out; they pursue him with elephants, with cattle-carts, with chariots, and with other single-hoofed animals. Then two lute-players follow after him and sing: "He has given," "He has sacrificed," "He has done that well," O Brāhmaṇa.

"Thus," "with antelope skins," "you fought," "you slew in that battle," "he performed such valor"—thus does the Brāhmaṇa sing the *iṣṭa* (the sacrifice), while the Rājanya sings the battle; the Brāhmaṇa sings the gift, while the Rājanya sings the valor. A Brāhmaṇa takes the name "Vīna" (the lute-player); he is not a friend of the Rājanyas. One of the two sings three verses, the other sings three; thus these two sing them forth.
They sing for a year with the *va* and *pra* syllables alone, as time after time arrives. Thus [ends the section].

Then, having offered the *sāvitra* oblation, he places the fire-pan (*ukhā*) on the fire. He performs the entire ritual procedure for the fire (*agnikarman*), and does not omit any part of the fire-ritual. He begins with the first consecration-oblations (*dīkṣāhuti*). He follows this twenty-one-fold consecration with the formula: "Svāhā to the resolved one (*adhim*), svāhā to the resolved upon (*ādhīta*), svāhā to Prajāpati, the resolved upon. [He continues] in this manner...

Having placed together the initiation of the sacrifice (*adhvaradīkṣā*), the initiation of the vital breath (*prāṇadīkṣā*), the initiation of the fire (*agnidīkṣā*), the initiation of the seasons (*ṛtudīkṣā*), the full-oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) as the seventh, and then the girdle, the black antelope horn, the staff of *udumbara* wood, the cup, and the offering of the vow (*vratapradāna*), he touches them with the first *dīkṣā-yoga*.

"Bhuvo devānāṃ karmaṇā—by means of the spring season, by the oblation, I consecrate myself with consecration"—with these words, he performs the black antelope skin consecration (*kṛṣṇājinadīkṣā*) in the same manner. He closes his two fists and restrains his speech, then announces the consecration. Then he says: "O consecrated one, restrain your speech; O consecrated one, release your speech. When his speech has been released, he goes out toward the north and offers a cake on eight potsherds to Savitṛ in the fires of the domestic priest (*purohita*).

Having caused it to be cooked and having placed it before him, he offers the fore-portion oblations: "Svāhā to Agni! Svāhā to Indra and Agni! Svāhā to Prajāpati! Svāhā to the Viśvedevas! Svāhā to all the deities!"

"To the deities, svāhā!"—having thus cut off the portion for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, he performs the secondary offerings (*upahoma*). There are twelve gallops, eighty-three horse-movements (*aśvacarita*), and four firm steps (*dhṛti*); these amount to four hundred. When that [offering] has been completed, at that very moment, he offers a cake on eleven potsherds to Savitṛ Prasavitṛ. For this [offering], these same [verses] are the secondary offerings. When that [offering] has been completed, at that very moment, [he offers] to Savitṛ Āsavitṛ.

[He prepares] a cake on twelve potsherds. For this [sacrifice], these very [oblations] are the secondary offerings (*upahoma*). When [the time for] the vow has arrived, having bestowed the vow, he restrains his speech. In the morning, when the sun has risen, having offered the oblation to Savitṛ, he places the fire-pan (*ukhā*) upon the fire and performs the entire ritual of the fire; he does not deviate from the ritual of the fire. He proceeds with the second set of initiation oblations: "To the body, svāhā! To whom, svāhā! To which one, svāhā!"...

He follows the *viṃśinī* initiation, discards the *agnidīkṣā*, and discards the seasonal (*ṛtu*) initiation; the fourth [offering] is the *pūrṇāhuti*. Then [he discards] the girdle and the black antelope horn.

Having placed nearby an *audumbara* staff, an *audumbara* cup, and the offering for the vow (*vratapradāna*), he touches them with the second consecration formula (*dīkṣāyoga*) while reciting: "Bhuvo devānāṃ rudrebhiḥ. The black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*) and the consecration are common [to all]. He makes the fist-closure; he restrains his speech and announces the consecration. Then he says: "O consecrated one, restrain your speech; O consecrated one, release your speech."

When she has been released, having gone northward, he offers an *aṣṭākapāla* cake to Savitṛ in the fires of the domestic priest; for this [offering], these very same [verses] are the *upahomīyās*. When that [offering] is completed, at midday, he offers an *ekādaśakapāla* cake to Savitṛ Prasavitṛ; for this [offering], these very same [verses] are the *upahomīyās*. When that [offering] is completed, in the afternoon, he offers a *dvādaśakapāla* cake to Savitṛ Āsavitṛ; for this [offering], these very same [verses] are the *upahomīyās*. When [the guest] has arrived, having given him the *vrata* food, he releases his speech.
When the vow has been undertaken, the Brāhmaṇa sings. When it has been released, the Rājanya [sings]. In this very same manner, he undergoes initiation for seven days.

Offering ever higher oblations and touching [the sacrificer] with ever higher applications of the *dīkṣā*, on the seventh day he begins with the final *dīkṣā*-oblations: "To Viṣṇu svāhā! To Viṣṇu, who has entered the earth, svāhā!"—this fourth [offering] is indeed the *pūrṇāhuti*. Then, having placed the girdle (*mekhalā*) nearby, he touches the *dīkṣā* with the highest application of yoga: "Bhuvaḥ... [K1 bh.]
With the verses beginning “To the great [goddess] of the gods” and “The good protector,” the initiation with the black antelope skin is performed in common. “Release [it],” he says.

On the eighth day, the *vātsapra* and *viṣṇukrama* rites are discontinued; however, the *vātsapra* and *viṣṇukrama* rites continue for him in his own fires. With these offerings, he sacrifices in the fires of the domestic priest (*purohita*); thus the sacrificer proceeds for twelve months and seven days. Wherever he was previously...

[It] carries away the world. Thus, they cause these [people] to congregate together: carpenters together, masons together, chariot-makers together, potters together, and smiths together. Their respective crafts are as follows: this, indeed, is the craft of the carpenters—

They erect aśvattha posts with their roots upwards, constructing a pen for the aśvatthas; they are mouth-deep, as deep as the thighs, or even as high as the thighs. There are four or eight indrāṇas; there are abhyārohas, śritīs, and a hundred fuel-sticks of bilva wood piled up, and twenty-one sacrificial posts.

There are two made of *rājjudāla* wood, two of *pautudāru*, six of *bilva*, six of *khadira*, and six of *pālāśa*; there are *pālāśa* [posts], and the *upaśaya* is of *pālāśa*. All of them are twenty-one *aratnis* in length.

Sixfold are the carts: the ascending cart, the kitchen cart, the high-status cart, the flowing cart, the chariot-carrying cart, and the drum-carrying cart. There are many such types; they prepare many kinds of *sruk* ladles, many *camasa* cups, and many *pātrī* bowls.
There too, they fashion that vessel from the wood of the supreme tree; thirty-six long-handled ladles (*sruva*), thirty-six gourd-spoons (*alābu-darva*), and thirty-six small spoons (*aṣṭama*).
This is the work of bamboo-workers (*veṇukāra*); this is added here. These are the many things they fashion as armor and chariot-fendering shields. This is the work of chariot-makers (*rathakāra*).

They fashion many new chariots, complete with rims. This is the great variety of potters: they produce a great quantity of vessels the size of jars, a great quantity of jars, and a great quantity of pots.
There too, they prepare those three *kuṃbhī* vessels which would suffice for a cow cut limb by limb, just as there are twenty-one kinds of bricks. This is the work of the smiths:

They fashion vessels of gold and silver for the *mahiman* cups: a golden *rukma*, a golden *kaśipu*, and seven or eight [cups] weighing a hundred *palas*. There are four *vidhavana* vessels made of gold with silver handles, or silver ones with golden handles. There are six *kamaṇḍalu* vessels made of gold with silver bands, or silver ones with golden bands.

The side-pieces (aupaśaya) are made of gold with silver pins, or silver with golden pins; the head-ornament (kurīra) is made of gold with a silver knot, or silver with a golden knot; the halter is threefold; the foot-tether is threefold; and whatever else is on both sides of the horse, all that is threefold and made of gold. There are a hundred golden daggers.
There were one hundred silver shafts with silver nocks, one hundred golden shafts with golden nocks, thirty-six iron shafts, and four black-iron shafts with black-iron nocks.

All the other *sarava* arrows are black with black shafts, while the golden ones have golden shafts; these two sets amount to two hundred and forty-two swords that have been prepared; and there are one thousand silver [arrows] together with gold...
Three hundred and thirty-three golden needles, one thousand silver ones, and one thousand from the ocean; and three hundred and thirty-three golden needles, and three hundred...
And thirty-three silver [objects], three hundred and thirty-four iron ones, an iron water-pot, a mat of reeds, a garment of *tārpya* wool, and tenfold food.

Whatever honey there is in his kingdom, all that they collect together... they send forth kingdoms: a hundred skins of ghee, a hundred skins of honey... a hundred skins of rice. A hundred skins of honey... a hundred skins of rice. [Repeated fragments: ...kingdoms... ghee... a hundred skins of honey... [and so on].

(9) One hundred rice-skins; one hundred broad-grain skins; one hundred parched-rice skins; one hundred *karamba*-skins; one hundred fried-grain skins; one hundred flour-skins; one hundred lentil skins; and one [skin] of *priyaṅgu* rice grains.

Regarding the skins—then they bring these animals to him, both domestic and wild, including barren cows... [of those] brought and not yet brought, [he assigns them] to the *adhvaryu*... of those, whichever he considers to be obtainable, they guard. Those which are fit for cooking... [he cooks].
They cook those who are to be cooked, and they slaughter those who are to be slaughtered.

In the sixth month, they do not keep the horse confined in the Vraja, but rather at this very *aśvattha* tree. While it stands there, six hundred men provide it with fodder for six months. On the full moon day, he performs the *āgamanīyā* sacrifice. If the horse should [return...]

And if it should be known as "future," and if it should indeed be known as "future," he offers with both [formulas]. If it is future, he should scatter [the grains] upon the *daśala*-fires; he should scatter them upon the *daśala*-fires: on the *gārhapatya*, the *anvāhāryapacana*, and the *āhavanīya*. Then, having scratched twelve potsherds for the *vaiśvānara* [offering], [he proceeds] with the twelve potsherds of the *bhracyā*...
Thus [it is said]: "The twelve-potsherd [offering]... [In this regard, having scratched out the twelve potsherds with a staff...]

Having cooked [the oblation], he sets it down. There are fifteen *sāmidhenī* verses; the two *ājyabhāga* offerings are the *vārtraghna*; [the principal offering is] Vaiśvānara: "Vaiśvānara has ascended the firmament in ancient fashion; the buffalo-bulls have seized him in the lap of the waters. The subjects have supported the king, the one worthy of praise. Mindful, Mātariśvan brought forth from Vivasvat the Vaiśvānara Agni... (RV 6.8.4). Thus.
Now, this very [teaching] was [received] by Śrutaśena Pārikṣita when he performed the Aśvamedha sacrifice. His horse, it is said, fell away [from the track].

He had performed the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*), but on that day a tiger killed his horse that had strayed away. He then performed this *iṣṭi* sacrifice for the recovery of the horse. Having brought back a golden axe, he said: "This much was the cost of the horse-recovery sacrifice; had I lived [longer], the horse would have returned."

This very [cow], known as the *āśvāgamanīyā* (the one that brings the horse), goes indeed to that very place where they offer these oblations. When she has settled there, they do not confine the horse in a stall made of *aśvattha* wood at that very moment; while he stands there, they bring fodder for him and these [attendants] wait upon him for seven days.
The domestic priest performs these sacrifices with these offerings in the fires. At this point, they employ these various sections (anuvākas):

the *ādhītayajus* section, the *aṅgahomas*, the *yajuṣaṅgahomas*, the two *aśvarūpa* sections, the *oṣadhihoma*, the *vanaspatihoma*, the *santanīs*, the *abhidhānas*, the *saṃplavas*, and the *khārihoma*.

Having offered these *dhṛti* oblations, they offer them nine times on the final day. He performs all the first [sets], all the middle [sets], and all the last [sets]. Having returned, he measures out the altar (*vedi*) as double its size, [constructing] the fire-altar (*agni*) in twenty-one layers (*ekaviṃśatividha*).
Now, these hundred human [bricks] have been prepared for him:

There were three hundred princes, clad in armor made of both metals, fully equipped with their charioteers and having their protective fenders extended, each yoked to four horses; and there were three hundred non-princes, fully equipped but without charioteers, with their protective fenders extended, each yoked to three horses.

Three hundred chariot-leaders (*sūtagrāmaṇī*), unarmored and with their charioteers unarmored, with their protective fenders spread out and their yokes doubled; three hundred *kṣattṛ*-gathers, with their foot-soldiers on bypaths; three hundred triple-bowmen; three...
Six hundred men with quivers, three hundred with sacred threads, and three hundred with staffs in hand and branches in hand—these twenty-four hundred men were prepared for him.

Then, as the sun sets, these princes set out in four divisions—seventy-five each toward every direction—and the people follow after them. They assemble in groups of three hundred chariots and three hundred foot soldiers for each direction. For that night, they remain there, staying vigilant and guarding themselves.

On the morning when the purchase of the horse is completed, having performed that, having piled the Gārhapatya altars and having placed them in position, and having offered the oblations to Nirṛti, he pours out the *prāyaṇīya* oblation. Having released his speech at the call for the preparer of the oblation (*haviṣkṛt*), he says to those who examine the horse: "Inquire what is done for the horse and what is not done."

"They should conquer for thirteen days," they say, "until the time of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). Regarding this, however, they also say: "In that case, nothing at all would remain; they should conquer for only one day. It is for only one day that they cause [the sacrifice] to succeed.

That which makes itself known as a commoner is not defeated; but that which does not make itself known is defeated, and that which does not make itself known will suffer total ruin. Now, those whom the Adhvaryu causes to be terrified, he sends forth after having first instructed them.

"Tell my Adhvaryu: 'Let him cut the Rajjudāla wood for the central fire-pit'; tell my Adhvaryu: 'Let him take the portions from the horse on the northern side'; tell my Adhvaryu: 'Let him cut the portions of the horse on a mat of Vetasa reeds'; tell my Adhvaryu: 'Let him take the portions of the horse with a golden vessel that has a golden handle.'"

"Rājjudāla wood for the *agniṣṭha* fire"—thus indeed it was said. In the kingdom of Janamejaya, there was a carpenter named Vaiśyavraja; there the *prāyaṇīya* sacrifice concludes with the *śaṃyu* formula.

He offers an oblation on a footprint leading to the couch; he steps upon the footprint. He purchases the King (Soma); having purchased the King, he milks the cow for him and prepares the *ātithya* (guest-offering), which concludes with the *iḍā*. There are twelve *upasads*; following each *upasad*, the twenty-one-fold fire-altar (*agni*) is built. On its day of preparation (*upavasatha*), they do not interrupt the consecration (*abhiṣeka*).

On the following day, having performed the final *pravargya* and *upasad* rites, he discards the fire according to the procedure for the fire (*agner āvṛtā*). They level the *sadas* and *havirdhāna* sheds; having crossed over the *pṛṣṭhya* cords, they cause them to enter together into the *havirdhāna* sheds.

Having brought forward the two Havirdhāna carts for the transport of the chariot, he traces around the pit for the Audumbarī post, the Uparava pits, and the pit for the sacrificial post (yūpa). He erects the Sadas shed and sets up the Āgnīdhra shed. Having performed the rites with the Uparavas, he pours out the earth for the Dhiṣṇiya hearths; he assigns the Anudeśyas and they spread the sacrificial grass (barhis). He leads forward King Soma, and having led forward Agni and Soma, he... [kā... Having led [the fire], he joins it with the *sara* by means of yoga—[thus K4, K1: having led...; M: having led...]—"Who joins you? May He join you," with these six [verses] he joins the middle enclosing-stick (*paridhi*), with five the southern one, and with five the northern one; he then releases the intermediate consecration (*avāntaradīkṣā*).

Having erected the sacrificial post made of *rājjudāla* wood with the fire at its base, he dedicates the animal for Agni-Soma. Having offered its omentum and performed the ritual purification (*mārjana*), he offers the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) belonging to the animal sacrifice.

The oblations of the *devasū* follow that; there is a sacrifice (*iṣṭi*) consisting of ten oblations. For the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*), the call is given as "Recite! and "Sacrifice! For the other oblations, it is performed in a low voice (*upāṃśu*). The call for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering is common to all, as is the *iḍā*. Having performed the animal sacrifice and having carried around the *vasatīvarī* waters, they leave over the milks and fast. In the morning, having washed their hands, he offers the *sāvitra* oblation at midday.

Then, having taken the portions of clarified butter (ājya) and brought down the King Soma, he begins the morning litany (prātaranuvāka). When the morning litany has been concluded, he says "avocad" (he has spoken), pours out water, offers the residue (saṃsrāva) into the Āhavanīya fire, and having performed the Agniṣṭoma rite, he enters the sacrificial ground. He offers the curd-draught (dadhighraha) dedicated to Prajāpati. The pressing is straightforward, and the cups (graha) are those belonging to the Agniṣṭoma, as is well known.

As soon as the *adhvaryu* has drawn the cups, they lead this horse, having washed it in the southern pool, up to the northern corner of the altar behind the tail; they station it facing north, and they enclose it to the north of the *āstāva* with a shed that has three doors on the front side, while the cups have already been drawn.

The *adhvaryu* takes up five bundles of sacrificial grass (*barhis*) and three hundred-pala gold pieces. Having grasped the horse's tail, they proceed to the *bahiṣpavamāna* chant; at the place of chanting (*āstāva*), the horse runs out, and for it he throws down a bundle of grass and a hundred-pala piece. He gives the bundle of grass to the *udgātṛ*, the bundle of grass to himself, and then says: "O *udgātṛ*, I shall give you a hundred cows and a hundred-pala piece as a lower gift."

"Let the horse sing the *udgītha*," he said. "So be it," replied the *udgātṛ*. They lift him up; they carry forward the enclosure for the one who draws first, and they prepare the others. Just as one might cry out upon seeing someone after not having seen them for a long time, so does he cry out; the others leap forward. They consider this to be the *udgītha*, and this the *upagīta*.

"‘The horse has become pure,’ they say; ‘It has attained long life, it has attained good offspring, it has attained preeminence among its kin, it has attained all that is auspicious for this sacrificer who presses the soma. He leads the other [oxen] forward to the half [of the altar], directing them toward the eastern direction.
Then, having brought this horse and stationed it in its proper place, he fastens it with a triple-strand rope, binds it with a triple-strand foot-halter, and scatters grain around its hoof-ring.

Then he said, "O Udgātṛ, I shall give you a hundred oxen and a hundred palas of gold; sing the *udgītha* thus! "So be it," replied the Udgātṛ. Before the *bahiṣpavamāna* chant, three hundred cows and three hundred palas of gold arrived as the *stotra* was being performed.

The Udgātṛ chants the Bahiṣpavamāna. Having chanted, while rising, he issues the command: "O Āgnīdhra, spread the fires; bring the sacrificial animals near. Having taken the Āśvina cup and gone out, he recites for the one being girt with the cord; he speaks eleven times at the Agniṣṭha post.

He winds eleven girdles around [the sacrificial posts]; he dedicates eleven animals of the *ekādaśinī* set. First are those belonging to the Aśvamedha: the animal for Agni with a black neck, and the ewe for Sarasvatī—these are they. Having offered their omenta and having performed the ritual purification (*mārjana*), they proceed to the procession.

This Agniṣṭoma sacrifice is extended as a Catuṣṭoma with the Rathantara as its Pṛṣṭha-stotra. For it, the Bahiṣpavamāna is performed on four verses; the Ājya-stotras on eight; the Mādhyandina-pavamāna on twelve; the Pṛṣṭha-stotras on sixteen; the Ārbhava-pavamāna on twenty; and the Yajñāyajñiya on twenty-four.

The straight morning pressing is concluded; the straight midday pressing proceeds. They sit down for the *nārāśaṃsa* cups. When the *nārāśaṃsa* cups have been set down, he offers the *āptī* oblations into the Āhavanīya fire while about to offer the sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*) for the priests. These are the eight spoonfuls with the formula: "May the sacrifice come hither."

Then, having offered the *dakṣiṇās*, he gives a third part of what has been won, according to his faith; having given of his own property and assigned it, and having offered the *vaiśvakarmaṇa* oblations, he offers the *paryāpti* oblations into the *āhavanīya* fire with the nine *sruva*-oblations beginning with "The past, the present, the future. He takes the *vastīvarī* waters on his back. The midday pressing concludes straightway.

The third pressing concludes with straightness. This is the fourfold *agniṣṭoma*. Having performed the *anūyāja* offerings with the formula, "O Brahman, we shall set forth," he offers the *svaru* chips. Then, having proceeded with the *hāryojana* offerings, they proceed with the *apsuṣoma* offerings. Then, having gone back westward, [he performs the offerings] for the wives with the tail-flesh portions.

They perform the *saṃyāja* offerings. Having joined hands with the wives, they go eastward and offer the *taraṃsī* oblations. Having offered the *taraṃsī* oblations, he replenishes the *dhruvā* ladle and pours [the remainder] into the *ājyasthālī*.

They erect this level enclosure with a pillar of *rājjudāla* wood fixed toward the fire; they provide for it a single entrance from the west; they erect the supporting beams, they carry forward the walls, and they turn the *indrāṇacāila* pillar toward the one fixed at the fire.

(16) Those twenty-one [bricks] which the Adhvaryu alone offers with a *yajus* formula—on two of them the *pāṃsūmāva* are placed; those nineteen [bricks] which the Adhvaryu alone offers with a *yajus* formula, the Pratiprasthātṛs offer silently. Then he offers the *khārī* oblations: with "To Datvat, svāhā! for the food, and with "To Adantaka, svāhā! for the clarified butter; then the *anuvāka*; then the *khārī* oblation. M], they ascend so that the youngest may not be left behind; having descended, carried around the *vasatīvarī* waters, and distinguished the milks, they ascend after either eating or drinking them—or rather, having drunk the water, they ascend.

Beginning from the first section (*anuvāka*) of the preceding sections, they proceed with the concluding formulas (*samāpti*). They conclude this first section of concluding formulas with clarified butter alone, reciting in a forward direction: "Svāhā to one! Svāhā to two! Then he offers the *khārī*-oblation: "Svāhā to the toothed! Svāhā to the toothless!"—this is with clarified butter; then [he recites] the section.

Now follows the *khārī* oblation. One performs the *khārī* oblation with clarified butter alone, interweaving it with the *anuvākas* by means of the *khārī* oblation. When they arrive at the point where [the text says], "To the end, svāhā! To the further half, svāhā!"—from that point on, they turn back. Thus, performing the sacrifice night after night until the conclusion is reached, they remain engaged in the oblations.

Until the Prātaranuvāka, the two Adhvaryus ascend the time for the Prātaranuvāka, saying, "These two lying down [fires] are the last Anuvāka. Then they descend; the two lying down [fires] proceed from there. The Adhvaryu alone offers the lying down [fire] with a Yajus formula, while the Pratiprasthātṛ offers silently. Having descended and washed his hands, the Adhvaryu offers the oblation to Savitṛ at midday.

Then, having taken the portions of clarified butter and having brought down the King Soma, he introduces the Prātaranuvāka. Once the Prātaranuvāka has been introduced, the two Adhvaryus climb up, saying, "This is the final recitation," and then they descend; thereafter, the two Adhvaryus proceed with the Upaśaya bricks.

They continue offering in this very manner until the *paridhānīyā* verse. When the time for the *paridhānīyā* arrives, they place the two *upaśaya* logs [K4 reads *eśayau*] down, saying: "This is the final *anuvāka*."

Having spoken thus and brought the king forward, he begins the morning litany (*prātaranuvāka*). Once the morning litany has been commenced, they both ascend; the Adhvaryu says, "This is the final *anuvāka*," and they both descend. Then the two Adhvaryus take their respective positions. While they are thus offering oblations, they continue to offer until the time for the concluding verse (*paridhānīyā*). At the time of the concluding verse, they both ascend; the Adhvaryu says, "This is the final *anuvāka*," and they both descend. Then the two Adhvaryus take their respective positions at the two lying-offerings (*upaśaya*).

Having descended, he offers before the *paridhānīyā* verse, saying: "Svāhā to Uṣas! Svāhā to the Dawn! Svāhā to her who is about to rise! When the *prātaranuvāka* has been concluded with the *paridhānīyā* itself as the fourth [verse], he gazes at the waters. Having poured out the water, [he pours it] into the *āhavanīya* fire.

Having offered the remnants from the *vyavānīya* and *āhavanīya* fires, having performed the *ukthya* sacrifice, he enters [the ritual space]. He offers the *dadhi-graha* belonging to Prajāpati; having taken the *nigrābhya* waters that have been spoken over with the *śukra* cup, and having drawn the *ādābhya* [Soma] with the formula, he hands it over to another.

Then, having taken the *upāṃśusavana* stone, he measures out the King [Soma]; he draws the *prāṇagraha* cups; he follows the first spotted [cups]. Having measured the subsequent measure silently, he draws the *apānagraha* cups; he follows the later spotted [cups].

Having taken the *aṃśu* cup, he offers it. Then he offers the *adābhya* cup; he gives whatever sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) belongs to those two. Having performed the ritual action for the *upāṃśu*, he offers the *upāṃśu*. The King (Soma) has been pressed and poured into the *droṇakalaśa* jar. Then he awaits the rising sun; when the sun has fully risen, he offers: "To the one rising, svāhā! To the one having risen, to all, svāhā!"

Where he offers with the formula, "Svāhā to all!"—this is what those who know the Aśvamedha prepare for. Now, therefore, there is indeed an inquiry into this. Regarding this they say: "The Upāṃśu and Antaryāma [libations] are indeed the out-breath and the in-breath, and the clarified butter (ājya) is the thunderbolt. If he were to offer the butter-oblation between the Upāṃśu and Antaryāma, he would sever his own out-breath and in-breath with the butter-thunderbolt."

"One should separate them," they say. Regarding this, they further say: "The Upāṃśu and Antaryāma cups are indeed out-breath (prāṇa) and in-breath (apāna); the clarified butter (ājya) is food. Food does not injure breath; therefore, one should certainly offer it. Moreover, they also say: "The Upāṃśu and Antaryāma cups are indeed out-breath and in-breath; the clarified butter is breath. Breath does not injure breath; rather, by means of it, he becomes more abundant. Therefore, one should certainly offer it."
He indeed offers it; such is the established rule.
They distribute it. Regarding that food which remains after the city has been traversed, of that there are four portions.

(7) Having removed four winnowing baskets for grain, they carry everything else to the Adhvaryu’s dwelling. When the sun has risen, he offers the Antaryāma cup; he offers to Raśmi. The cups are drawn in the established manner up to the Āgrayaṇa. Having drawn the Āgrayaṇa, he draws the two Mahiman cups with vessels of gold and silver, using the [verses] "He who breathes" and "He who gives life," reciting them with the *upayāma* formula and without the *yonis*. He deposits them.

Then he draws this *prājāpatya* *somagraha* as an *atigrāhya*, using a vessel made of *pālāśa* wood, with the verse, “In the beginning, the Golden Germ (Hiraṇyagarbha) evolved. He sets it down with a support (*upayāma*) and a base (*yoni*). Then he draws three *pṛṣṭhya* cups. Now, regarding this, some draw them separately day by day, saying, “But one should indeed draw them here”; however, he draws them here. This is the established rule.

Then he draws the *ukthya* cup; having wiped the *dhruva* and the jars, he offers the oblation of drops, offers the *santati* oblations, and they chant the *pavamāna* hymn. Having risen when the chanting is finished, he issues the command: "O *Āgnīdh*, spread the fires; bring the animals close. Having drawn the *āśvina* cup and gone out, he recites the invitatory verse for the one being girded with the sacrificial cord, and says: "Twenty-four... [K1, K4: ...]

He winds twenty-four cords around the post standing nearest the fire, each with a separate knot; he hides the wooden pegs within them. Then, having raised the southern post made of *pūtudāru* wood, he winds four cords around it, each with a separate knot; he hides the wooden pegs within them, each in its own place.

In this very way he erects the northern post made of *pūtudāru* wood; he encircles it with four girdles, each with a different kind of fruit, and into each of them he inserts a different kind of *svaru*.

Three *bilva* logs to the south, three to the north; three *khadira* logs to the south, three to the north; three *pālāśa* logs to the south, three to the north. Upon these, he winds four ropes each. They have different origins; upon them, he inserts the fire-sticks (*svaru*) as if they were distinct.

On the southernmost *pālāśa* post, he ties a long girdle (*raśanā*) which reaches down to the northernmost post; having brought that [girdle] right here and laid it aside, he places to the south of the southernmost *pālāśa* post a bed (*upaśaya*) facing east, and silently fastens the girdle upon it. He places for it a handful of sacrificial grass (*barhis*), a chip from the sacrificial post (*yūpa-śakala*), and the *svaru* chip.

Then, having taken two blades of sacrificial grass (*barhis*) with the formula "For food (*iṣe*) thee," and having offered the two introductory oblations, he dedicates the animals: a goat for Agni, one for Pūṣan, a castrated ram, a Gomṛga antelope, and one for Indra and Pūṣan—thus six. Eight remain from this section; those make fourteen. With the formula "To Agni Anīkavant, a red-marked ox," there are eleven; those make twenty-five.

With the formula, "For Soma, the self-ruling king, two oxen that draw the cart," eighteen young, tender calves are sacrificed at the Agniṣṭha post—one from each of the forty-nine fires. On the southern post, he performs the introductory rite for the offering to Indra-Agni with wood from the *pūtudāru* tree; on the northern post, he does so for the offering to Agni-Indra.
"Rohita, dhūmrarohita"—these are eighteen; of these, he first dedicates nine to the Aindrāgna deities on the south, and the remaining nine to the Āgnendra deities on the north.

The sets with Indra and Agni as the tenth are completed on the south, and those with Agni and Indra as the tenth on the north; the barren cows and the hornless ones follow the northernmost [posts]. Then he dedicates the wild animals: "For Indra the King, the boar. Of these, they hold six in front to the south of the central post in the open spaces, and five behind in the northern ones.

Then he dedicates this undefined *sūkara* animal belonging to Prajāpati while it is still visible; regarding its dedication, they say: "By its dedication, everything here—whatever there is—becomes dedicated. Having dedicated it, he offers an oblation with the formula: "To the one dedicated, svāhā!"

Then they turn their own chariot around; having stationed it facing east along the path of the *camasa*-bearers, to the north of the two *havirdhāna* sheds and to the south of the *āgnīdhra*, they stretch the canopy over it. Whatever its ornamentation may be...

He adorns it with that ornament. Then, having brought this horse that has been presented, he yokes it to the southern pole with the verse: "They yoke the ruddy, bright one as he moves about, standing on all sides. A messenger raises the northern pole for him with the verse: "Making a banner for those who have no banner. He fastens the standard and arms the sacrificer with the armor using the *anu-vāka* for donning armor.
Thus [ends the section].

With one verse, "The appearance is like that of a cloud," he takes up the bow; having strung it with one verse, he strokes the string with one; with one verse he touches the two ends of the bow; with one verse he covers the quiver; with one verse he raises the reins; with one verse he consecrates the horses; with one verse [he addresses] the chariot and its equipment.

He gazes at the others; with two [verses] he pays homage to the Pitṛs from the south; with two he performs the drawing of the arrow; with one he pulls out the whip; with one he throws the hand-guard around; with three he mounts; with three he strikes the drum for the warrior. Nine milkings are there for this man... his head is shattered, and his private parts are destroyed. Doha... humans... [M379] K4, M: parekṣete; K1: ... (23) nmūrdhā hāsya vipa .e . thopastham; M: doha . . . [end of fragment].

(7) A human being ought to stand firm; he who would mount it—his head shall fall off. Having placed his hand upon the seat with these [verses], he should maintain [the position]; thus [it is called] the *rathopastha*.

Having thus placed his hand upon these [stones], he holds them. Having caused him to go out between the *cātvāla* and the *utkara*, they proceed toward the southern goal (*kāṣṭhā*) of the lake, with the verses: "The steed has stepped forth; the steed has stepped upon the earth. O Savitṛ, those paths of yours which lead to the day... He causes the horse to step forward with the verses beginning with "He has come with cooked offerings" and "Whatever [sin] the waters have gone away from."

"(4) ... came unto you"; M: "... Savitṛ ... (19) ... (14) came unto you. At this very point, while the horse stands, he touches its shoulder-blade (*śakunisāda*) with the verse for greatness: "Heaven is your back, earth your seat."

He strokes the right side down to the fetlocks; they turn the horse toward the south. While it is being turned, he makes [the sacrificer] recite: "O praiser, turn this horse back along this path... [The verse continues]. They do not let go of him; then he gives this [horse] to the *adhvaryu*, or to the deputy of the *adhvaryu*. This is his legal share (*dhārmya*). They keep the horse right here.

Then they lead forth the wives; the chief queen goes first with a hundred princesses. They bring a thousand golden glass beads, *kāsāmbava* ointment, and a hundred silver glass beads for the king’s anointing. [The charioteer], the *kṣattṛ*, and the *saṃgrahītṛ* [follow].

(28) With a hundred charioteers and collectors, the King [acted] toward the charioteers and collectors of the Magadhas, together with their wives. A discarded woman was brought forth, bringing a thousand sea-born glass beads and that unguent. That which was ancient, from the time of the former king, the Queen, together with a hundred princesses, was weaving a thousand golden glass beads, saying "Bhūr! ten by ten.
Ten women each weave ten glass beads toward the west.

As before, they weave a thousand silver *kāca* beads with the other [strings], ten in each single braid, saying, "Bhuvaḥ. Then they weave a thousand ocean-born (*sāmudra*) *kāca* beads with the other [strings], ten in each single braid, saying, "Śuvaḥ. Then they anoint him; that which is from the chest forward, [the Queen] with a hundred princesses...

He lies down with the Kāsāmbava princesses, [saying]: "May the Vasus anoint you with the Gāyatrī metre," as he does that which is westward from the chest and eastward from the navel with the Kāsāmbava [ointment].

"Let the *vāvātā* anoint you along with the others, O *udrā*, with the *traiṣṭubha* metre"—with this, she anoints with *gaulgulava* resin that part which is behind the navel; the *parivṛktī* anoints the entire rear half along with the others, saying, "Let the *ādityas* anoint you with the *jāgata* metre"—with this, she anoints with *mauṅsa* resin. Then, while he stands right there, they scatter these winnowing baskets for him: the *mahiṣī*, the *vāvātā*, and the *parivṛktī*.
They cause the discarded wife to eat the portions of the *asitāni* that are held before her face, making her smell them.

"Lājīñ chācī = Prajāpati. They say that whichever [cow] should smell the first [portion], her offspring would be the best; if one should smell the *māhānasī* [cow], the offspring of whichever [cow] the sacrificer desires would be the best. This [cow] turns toward the sacrificer. Then, having brought this horse and placed it in its proper place, they do not scatter [the grain] into winnowing baskets for him.

<11.19> Then, having performed the rite with the well-known fire produced by friction (*nirmanthya*) and having struck the post, he makes the oblation. Then, taking the ropes with the formula, "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ," they bind the animals: those at the post nearest the fire (*agniṣṭha*), both the Adhvaryu and the Pratiprasthātṛ; the Pratiprasthātṛ [binds] the others for the Pratiprasthātṛ. Having bound the principal animal of those dedicated to the same deity to the post, they tie the others to it.

Regarding the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), they attach the victim; however, one does not yoke eight of the domestic animals, nor any of the wild ones. Then, having wound this long rope around it, he ties it to the northern post; by means of that, all his animals become yoked—both those domestic animals which he does not yoke and all the wild ones.

Having bound them, he offers oblations, saying, "To the one seized, svāhā!"—thus, "To the one seized, svāhā! Those who have swords in their hands stand behind them: those who possess a hundred gold [swords] with silver hilts stand to the south of the *agniṣṭha* post, while those who possess a hundred silver [swords] with golden hilts [stand to the north].

With those [shafts] made of gold, which are to the north; with those thirty-six made of iron, for Kṛṣṇa; with four shafts made of black iron, for Kṛṣṇa; with those shafts made of iron, which are at the rear; and with the arrow smeared with poison, [he pierces] the horse.

Then, having taken up the sprinkling waters (*prokṣaṇī*), they sprinkle the animals. Those that are at the fire-altar (*agniṣṭha*), the Adhvaryu and the Pratiprasthātṛ sprinkle; the Pratiprasthātṛ [sprinkles] the others for the Pratiprasthātṛ. He sprinkles the animal dedicated to Agni and the one dedicated to Pūṣan in the established manner. Then he sprinkles the horse. Wherever he sprinkles the horse, he follows [the ritual action] with the verse: "The seed was born; Parjanya is the rain-giver."

26. Then, when the Adhvaryu causes him to smell the water, he addresses it with: "Agni was the victim; with him they sacrificed. They conquered that world in which Agni [is established]; that is your world—conquer it, therefore, and smell [the water]. Vāyu! Āditya! [K4,78a9] Thus.

Now, when Śrutasena Pārikṣita performed this very sacrifice—the Aśvamedha—at that time Kratvāsthira Kāvya was his Adhvaryu priest. At that moment, he (the horse) addressed him by means of a sniffing-salutation (*avaghrāṇa*): "The fire was the victim; therefore, sniff at it! Vāyu [was the victim]; Āditya [was the victim]."
Then Vṛṣamantra Śaṃyuva came and sat down to the south; at that time, he consecrated with a mantra a new horse with a new nose-rope.

"Agni was the sacrificial animal; with him he sacrificed. He won this world in which Vāyu [or Agni] dwells. That is your world; therefore, I shall enter within you if you do not sniff at me—Vāyu, Āditya! He did not sniff at him. Then Vṛṣamantra said: "How could he possibly sniff at him, when the Adhvaryu shows him nothing but death, not a world? The King said to him:

"If you were the *adhvaryu*, you should smell [the offering]," he said. "Bring it here! he replied. "Even if you are being pulled away by many, tear them asunder and smell it," he said. "You are my *adhvaryu*," he said to him. Kāpya drove him away. Then Kāpya spoke in reply to him:

"But as for you, who—thinking, 'I shall lead him away for two days,' though he is not one whose *soma* has been pressed—did not lead him away at all from among the intermediate sacrificial gifts; then the King commanded the slaughterers: 'Wherever the Adhvaryu causes him to smell the water...'"

"Do not smell it! You must eat it!"—thus he spoke. At that time, he consecrated it with a sniff: "The fire was the animal; in which the sun is, that is your world. You shall conquer it if you sniff it; [it is] the wind, [it is] the sun."

Being pulled away by many, he tore them apart and smelled them; thus, this is both smelling and not-smelling. If he should desire, "May I not smell," he should consecrate them with the non-smelling [formula], and he indeed does not smell. But if he should desire, "May I smell," he should consecrate them with the smelling [formula].
Even when being pulled away by many, he pulls them toward himself and smells them.
It is well known that they sprinkle the others repeatedly, bringing the *prokṣaṇī* waters again and again.

Having made him drink [the water], having sprinkled [him], and having set down the vessel, he recites the invitatory verses for the fire being kindled; when the verses have been recited, having stepped across, they anoint the sacrificial animals.

Those [portions] which are at the Agniṣṭha, the Adhvaryu and the Pratiprasthātṛ [anoint]; the Pratiprasthātṛ [anoints] the others. Having anointed the principal [portion] among those belonging to the same deity with the two *sruva*-ladles, they anoint the others according to the invocation. Having anointed the *dhruvā* and set it down, he chooses the *pravara*. The Hotṛ sits down;
being impelled, he takes up the two *sruca*-ladles and performs the *prayāja* offerings.

"Kindled, he anoints the hollow of the prayers"—with these [verses] the Hotṛ performs the *āprī* litany; with these he sacrifices. Regarding this they say: "His fuel-sticks are upright"; one should satisfy [the gods] with these [verses], for these, being deficient and redundant, pervade the horse belonging to Prajāpati. And regarding this they also say:

That is not appropriate, that one should satisfy the horse with other *āprī*-verses while its own *āprī*-verses exist; rather, one should satisfy the horse with the horse's own *āprī*-verses. Thus, he satisfies the horse with the horse's own *āprī*-verses.

Having sent forth [the Agnīdh], he offers eleven *prayāja* oblations. He pours the entire contents from the *upabhṛt* ladle into the *sruk* at the fourth and eighth [oblations], leaving one-eleventh remaining. Having offered ten, he steps across [the altar] with the mantra, "Whither the axes-handed ones... Just as with the *svaru*, they anoint the animals according to the axe.

Having anointed the *svaru* of those belonging to the same deity as the one placed at the fire with the principal *svaru*, they anoint the others as they happen to be available. Having held the *svarus* down and having set the two offering-ladles (*srucau*) in their respective places, he says, "Recite the invitatory verse for Agni. While his hand is raised, he runs around [the altar] and offers the five *apāvī* oblations, ending with the last *pāvya*.

Having set aside the *apāvya* grass, he moves forward [or follows], saying: "May the ram protect thee with its cooked offerings; may the red-necked goat [protect thee]. Having placed it down, he takes up the *unmuka* and the *āmuka* and proceeds toward the north. Following behind him are the domestic animals; they keep the wild animals right there. Then they take up the *tārpya* garment, the *kṛtyadhīvāsa* garment, and the golden disk (*rukma*).

[The Adhvaryu and the Pratiprasthātṛ] take hold of the gold, the skin-covering, and the sacrificial grass as a load, thinking, "This belongs to Agni. Both the Adhvaryu and the Pratiprasthātṛ take hold of them with the two omentum-spits (*vapāśrapaṇī*). The other [assistants] take hold of the Pratiprasthātṛ from behind. Having caused them to go out between the *cātvāla* pit and the rubbish-heap (*utkara*), they lead them forward in an orderly manner. Those on the southern side belong to Indra-Agni, those on the northern side belong to Agni-Indra; for these two, they belong specifically to Agni.

He touches one of the two bundles of sacrificial grass (*barhis*) with this very *yajus* formula. Then, while leading away the load of sacrificial grass from the others, he goes toward the northern part.

Then, going to spread a covering for the horse, he takes from the northern part and spreads a covering for the horse: a garment of fine silk (*tārpya*), a lower garment (*kṛtyadhīvāsa*), a golden ornament (*kurukma*), and a golden cushion (*kaśipu*). Whatever remains of the fine silk garment—

The remainder of the *tārpya* garment is left over. Having wound that [remainder] around the rope used for the sacrificial horse's immolation (*aśvasaṃjñapanī*), they cause the horse to be immolated. While it is being immolated, the *prastotṛ* priest stands to the north, worshipping with the *yāma* *sāman*, saying, "Do not let him make a cry; immolate him! Having said, "Announce when he has been immolated," he returns again and [offers] "To breath, svāhā!"

"Vayānāya svāhā"—with these words he offers oblations while the animal is being slaughtered. Having looked at the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*), he sits down to the east of the *rājjudāla* post standing nearest the fire. As they engage in the theological debate (*brahmodya*), the Brahman priest stands to the south and the Hotṛ priest to the north. Then the Hotṛ first asks him: "O Brahman, I ask you: what indeed..."
"What was there before? he reflects; "Brahmā was there at the beginning," he says, for Brahmā was indeed the first thought.

"Victory is yours, O Brahman," says the Hotṛ. "Victory is yours, O Her," says the Brahman. Then the Brahman asks him: "O Hotṛ, I ask you: who indeed wanders alone? The Hotṛ responds: "The Sun wanders alone. "Victory is yours, O Hotṛ," says the Brahman. "Victory is yours, O Brahman," says the Hotṛ. Then the Hotṛ [asks him].

He asks: “O Brahmin, I ask you: regarding the waters and the earth...? Brahmā responds: “...that which is supreme, that has been conquered by you, O Brahmin. [The other replies: “It has been conquered by you, O Brahmin.”

(27) “As much as is yours, O Brahmin,” says the Hotṛ; “Victory is yours, O Hotṛ,” says the Brahman. Then his victory becomes established, directed toward the north. Then they announce: “The king has won; it is broken open and unconquered. [End] 11.21. [Cf. Caland, *Dritte Mittheilung*, Nos. 90, 91, 92: pp. 197–9 = KS 380–2.]

Then, when the animals have been immolated, having offered the *saṃjñapta-homa*, they proceed. ... [they] proceed here; the *mahiṣī* [proceeds] here. They protect the *mahiṣī*. They protect the *mahiṣī*.

(20) First, the chief queen (*mahiṣī*) arrives, accompanied by one hundred princesses; three hundred and thirty-three women carry golden needles, garlands, and powders. Then, with one hundred wives of the subordinate kings (*arāja*), the favorite consort (*vāvātā*) arrives; three hundred and thirty-three women carry silver spoons (*sū*), garlands, and powders. With one hundred [wives] of the chamberlain (*kṣattṛ*)...

Then, together with their wives, [the women] of Magadha made grass mats; and [they brought] hundreds of iron needles, garlands, and powders. Having arrived, they famously nourished the sacrificial animals; having nourished the animals, they adorned the horse.

That which is east of the chest, that the Mahiṣī, together with a hundred princesses, having shaken with powders, covers with garlands. That which is west of the chest and east of the navel, that the Svāvātā, together with the others, having shaken with powders...
That which is behind the navel is the *parivṛktī*; she should take all that is on the other side, and having shaken it with powders, they cover it with garlands.

Having adorned the horse and shaking it as they lead it forth, the chief queen goes around it first, accompanied by a hundred princesses. Having cast aside her southern cares and having bared her southern thighs, she strikes them three times while moving about.

Having circumambulated three times in one direction, they circumambulate three times in the opposite direction, saying: "Thee, the beloved of hosts; thee, the beloved of treasures. Having circumambulated three times in that manner, and having again circumambulated three times back the other way, they sit down. With a hundred [wives], together with their wives—the favorite ones—he casts aside the leftward [objects], the leftward thoughts, and the naked left thighs.

Having struck them, they walk three times around them from left to right, saying, “*Gaṇānāṃ tvā...*,” and then sit down. Together with the wives of the attendants (*kṣattṛ*) and the charioteers (*saṃgrahītṛ*), as well as the *kārimāgadhas*, the *parivṛktī* throws both types of dice-baskets (*ādhī*) and both types of dice-pieces (*anūrū*) [into the fire], leaves them naked, and having struck them, they walk three times around them from left to right, saying, “*Gaṇānāṃ tvā...*,” and then sit down.

"At this time," they say, "one who knows thus and is learned in the Vedas should shake [the bowl] while thinking, 'May I not fall into the share of Yama; may I attain victory in the assembly of Yama.'"

[K4 adds here: "If he should be weary from walking around, having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvīta), sipped water, and walked around with one of these [women], saying 'Thee, the beloved of the hosts, the beloved of the treasures,' and having walked around three times, they sit down facing him in this world. Now, therefore, regarding the dice-betters, they say: 'Women are the dice-betters; the Brahman is the cloth for the dice. Indeed, in that world, in the assembly hall of Yama, they play at dice with portions of their good deeds.

Regarding this, they say: "A learned man (*śrotriya*) who possesses such knowledge might, by his very knowledge, cause someone to be seized by Yama; he would lose his share in Yama and suffer defeat in Yama’s assembly. If he should be seized for the purpose of being led away, he should put on the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvīta*), sip water, and walk around together with one of these [women].
"Thou art the beloved of the hosts, thou art the beloved of the treasures"—having thus gone around three times in the opposite direction and then again three times, they sit down.

34. Now, therefore, concerning the *śamyāpāsas* (the throwers of the wooden pins). They say, "The *śamyāpāsas* are women; by means of the *brahman*, for three days no one whatsoever who has recited the *Sāvitrī* should be rejected by you. Indeed, in former times, women used to serve as *prātiṣṇātrīs* (those who lead forward), but they did not desire their husbands.

Those whom they call the former "praṇāyyas"—the royal princes of kings, and the charioteers, village-headmen, chamberlains, and collectors of non-kings—were indeed born from those very *śamyāvāsa* trees that were beneficial to them.

Now, if the Adhvaryu should desire of a woman, "May a son who is worthy of honor (*praṇāyya*) be born to her," he should instruct her: "O you who are devoted to your husband, do not be fickle even toward your husband; at the throw of the *śamyā*, call upon that man. He whom she thus calls is one who is worthy of honor.

C: He considers it most praiseworthy (*praṇāyya*). Just as among the royal *yajña-kratu*s the Aśvamedha is the preeminent, even so does he who is born from this [sacrifice] stand out above his peers. Now, therefore, regarding the Abhimedhika rites: having enclosed the horse, they lead forth the Mahiṣī.
11.22. [Cf. Caland, Dritte Mittheilung, No. 93: pp. 199–200 = KS 382–3.]

Saying, "O Mother, the mother leads her to the dog," he causes her to lie down to the north of the horse. Saying, "O auspicious one, dweller of Kāmpīla," he covers her. Saying, "In the heavenly world, may you both cover yourselves," he pushes her back. He places his left thigh over her. He addresses her with the verse: "I have conceived a son who shall bring forth offspring; let us two extend ourselves. And: "The bull, the placer of seed, places the seed in the womb; he sets the penis in its place; having raised the thighs, he has struck the enemy utterly."
Then he reproaches her, saying, "O Amba, O Ambali, O Ambika! The sacrificer addresses her thus: "Raise her up; like one purifying a load of bamboo..."
